papers.title: Upper and Lower Bounds on the Complexity of Unit-Distance Graph Realization in $\mathbb{Z}^d$
papers.abstract: It is known that the problem of recognizing the existence of a unit-distance realization in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ for a graph $G$ is NP-complete. Here, assuming ETH, we give a sub-exponential lower bound of $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$ for this problem in $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $2^{\Omega(n^{2/3})}$ in $\mathbb{Z}^3$, and give an upper bound of $2^{O(n^{(d-1)/d} (\log n)^2)}$ for the time complexity with an explicit divide-and-conquer algorithm. This approach beats naive exhaustive search by a factor of $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{1/d})$ in the exponent. For 2 and 3 dimensions, our upper and lower bounds match to within a logarithmic factor.

papers.title: Matrix Samplers and Quantum-Proof Extractors: Their Correspondence and Almost-Optimal Constructions
papers.abstract: We establish an equivalence between matrix samplers and quantum-proof randomness extractors. The classical sampler--extractor equivalence is established by a seminal work of Zuckerman (Random Structures & Algorithms, 1997). Using this equivalence, we construct explicit strong matrix samplers with optimal randomness overhead and near-optimal sample complexity via constructing quantum-proof extractors. Specifically for matrix dimension $D$, accuracy $\varepsilon$ and failure probability $\delta\leq\varepsilon$, our matrix sampler uses $m+O_\alpha(\log(D/\delta))$ random bits and $O_\alpha(\varepsilon^{-2-\alpha}\log^{1+\alpha}(D/\delta))$ samples, for any constant $\alpha>0$. Compared with the matrix sampler of Xun and Zuckerman (CCC 2025), our construction has improvements in two aspects. Under the same optimal random seed length, we can replace the $\operatorname{poly} D$ dependence in the number of samples by $O(\log^{1-\gamma} D)$. Under the same scale of sample size, we can remove their $\log\log D$ factor in the length of the random seed. Our underlying strong quantum-proof extractor has output length $n-O_\alpha(a+\log(1/\eta))$ and seed length at most $(1+\alpha)\log a+(2+\alpha)\log(1/\eta)+O_\alpha(1)$ for $n$-bit sources with conditional min-entropy $n-a$ and error $\eta$. We also obtain strong quantum-proof extractors for every constant entropy rate, for any error as small as $2^{-\Omega(n)}$, having optimal seed length $O(\log(n/\eta))$ and output length $\Omega(n)$, improving previous constructions.

papers.title: Irreducibility Testing of Sparse Polynomials over Integers is NP-hard and Probabilistic Polynomial Time
papers.abstract: In this paper, we prove that irreducibility testing for sparse polynomials in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is coNP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. That is, there exists no polynomial-time irreducibility test algorithm unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$. We also provide an upper bound for this problem by demonstrating that the same irreducibility testing problem lies in $\mathsf{PP}\subseteq\mathsf{PSPACE}$; in other words, it can be solved in probabilistic polynomial time and, moreover, within polynomial space. The fact that $\mathsf{SparseIrred}_{\mathbb{Z}}\in\mathsf{PP}$ relies on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis result of Cureton--Thorner and on the uniform effective prime-ideal bound by Frei--Sofos--Widmer just posted recently.

papers.title: Decomposing Directed Graphs into Partial Orders is Hard
papers.abstract: Comparability graphs represent partial orders and provide natural building blocks for representing a graph as a union of simpler graphs. The analogous task in the directed setting is to represent a digraph as a union of partial orders. Aboulker et al. [arXiv, 2026] recently introduced the partial order decomposition number as a useful structural parameter in their study of tournaments. Formally, a partial order decomposition of a digraph $D$ is a cover of its arc set by transitive acyclic subdigraphs, each representing a strict partial order on the vertex set of $D$. The partial order decomposition number is the minimum number of such subdigraphs needed. We also consider the partitioning variant, in which every arc belongs to exactly one of the partial orders in the decomposition. We prove that, for every fixed $k\geq 2$, deciding whether a digraph admits a decomposition into at most $k$ partial orders is NP-complete, even for directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). For $k=2$, we reduce from NAE-3-SAT. For $k\geq 3$, we reduce from $k$-Coloring, and the reduction yields DAGs with triangle-free underlying graphs. Both reductions establish hardness for both variants. We further show that the minimum cover size and the minimum partition size can differ even on DAGs.

papers.title: UPP$^{\text{cc}}$ is Not Closed Under Intersection
papers.abstract: The sign rank of a ${\pm 1}$-valued matrix $A$ is the minimum rank of a real matrix that agrees with $A$ entrywise in sign. For every sufficiently large $d$, we give an explicit matrix $A$ with $2^{\Theta(d^2)}$ rows and columns and sign rank $\Theta(d)$ such that $A \land A$ has sign rank $2^{\Theta(d)}$. Here, $A \land A$ is the communication matrix of the problem obtained by evaluating $A$ on disjoint inputs and taking the conjunction of the results. As the logarithm of sign rank characterizes unbounded-error communication complexity, this implies that the communication class $\mathsf{UPP}^{\mathsf{cc}}$ is not closed under intersection. The starting point for our lower bound is Forster's method, which relates the sign rank of a matrix to the average margin of representations of its rows and columns by points and halfspaces. We study a continuous analog for conjunctions of inner-product sign tests on the unit sphere. Rotational symmetry connects this problem to polynomial sign representations, yielding an exponentially small upper bound on the average margin. This bound holds even when sign constraints are relaxed near the sign tests' decision boundary, allowing us to transfer it to explicit finite sign matrices arising from intersections of integer halfspaces.

papers.title: Explicit Reed-Solomon Subspace Designs: Optimal List and Line Decoding
papers.abstract: For any desired rate $R \in (0,1)$, and gap to list-decoding capacity $\varepsilon > 0$, we give an explicit $n^{O_{\varepsilon}(1)}$ time construction of Reed-Solomon codes over extension fields of size polynomial in the block length $n$ that can be list-decoded from a fraction $1-R-\varepsilon$ of errors with the optimal list-size of $O(\frac{1-R}{\varepsilon})$. We also give a simpler, strongly explicit construction of evaluation points for which the associated Reed-Solomon code can be list-decoded from $1-R-\varepsilon$ errors with list size $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$. We provide a deterministic list-decoding algorithm for both constructions running in time $O_{\epsilon}(1)\mathsf{poly}(n)$. In fact, our Reed-Solomon codes are near-optimal subspace-design codes over a subfield. Via known results, this directly implies the combinatorial list-decoding guarantee, as well as near-optimal list-recovery bounds. We also present a new reduction showing that the subspace-design guarantee also implies line decoding over the extension field itself, which then yields proximity gaps and mutual correlated agreement up to proximity parameter approaching the optimal $1-R$ radius. Compared to the recent algorithm of Brakensiek, Chen, Putterman, Zhang, and Zheng (2026), which list decodes every Reed-Solomon code over prime fields up to capacity, our approach achieves constant (in fact, near-optimal) list size rather than a polynomially growing one, at the cost of carefully choosing the code's evaluation points. In a companion paper, we show that these respective restrictions are unavoidable.

papers.title: Impossibility of No-Regret in Multi-Agent Bidding
papers.abstract: We consider $T$ repeated second-price auctions across $n$ pacing bidders with i.i.d. item arrivals, and show that it is computationally impossible for all bidders to achieve no-regret simultaneously while satisfying their respective budget or return-on-investment constraints. Therefore, in the prominent internet auction systems where buyers simultaneously deploy pacing algorithms or automated bidding agents, we cannot hope to achieve joint no-regret guarantees in general. We establish a deterministic relationship that high variance in online bidding systems implies high regret. By showing that one can extract a pacing equilibrium from a low-variance system, we prove PPAD-hardness of attaining joint no-regret. For several widely used bidding algorithms, we also show evidence from dynamical systems and numerical simulations that they can indeed display high-variance behavior through cycling, even on simple market instances.

papers.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
papers.abstract: It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so H{\aa}stad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-\Omega(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.

papers.title: An Unconditional Lower Bound for the Active-Set Method in Almost-Linear Programming
papers.abstract: We prove that, for every fixed $\epsilon\in(0,1]$, the active-set method requires exponentially many iterations in the worst case to maximize a convex objective of the form $(x_1)^{1+\epsilon}+\vec c^{\top}\vec x$ subject to linear constraints, regardless of the pivot rule used. Our lower bound therefore holds for objectives arbitrarily close to the linear case $\epsilon=0$, where the active-set method coincides with the simplex method and a lower bound for all pivot rules would constitute a major breakthrough. The special case $\epsilon=1$ yields a lower bound in convex quadratic maximization. This improves on the best previously known lower bound [IPCO 2025] requiring polynomial objectives of degree $\omega(\log d)$ in dimension $d$ and firmly resolves the open question of whether a constant degree suffices. Our result is based on a novel extended formulation, recursively constructed using deformed products. Its key feature is that it projects onto a polygonal approximation of a parabola while preserving all of its exponentially many vertices. We define a convex objective with a single non-linear variable that forces the active-set method to follow the parabolic boundary of this projection, without allowing any shortcuts along chords corresponding to edges of its full-dimensional preimage.

papers.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
papers.abstract: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $[N]$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted and collision detection is unavailable. Our neighborhood-clearing procedure reuses an elected receiver to secure its entire closed in-neighborhood in $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. Charging each distinct closed neighborhood once yields $\mathcal O(m\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds under an explicit degree-concentration condition, for every polynomial identifier range. A complementary adaptive-pruning procedure combines quadratic contraction with completion sensitive to the number of unsecured sources. If $a\ge1$ sources remain at completion entry, permutation selectors reduce the balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. A geometric execution attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+n\tau+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for a path cover of scale $k$, weight $\tau$, and $u$ exceptions. For directed graphs with common in- and out-degree $\Delta$, the portfolio achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrt\Delta,n^2/\Delta\})$. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs; degrees, covers, and structural constants are used solely in the analysis. The unrestricted polynomial-identifier density extension remains open.

papers.title: Almost-Polynomial Ratio Almost-ETH-Hardness of Approximating Densest $k$-Subgraph
papers.abstract: In the Densest $k$-Subgraph problem, given an undirected graph $G$ and an integer $k$, the goal is to find a subgraph of $G$ on $k$ vertices that contains maximum number of edges. Even though the state-of-the-art algorithm for the problem achieves only $O(n^{1/4 + \varepsilon})$ approximation ratio (Bhaskara et al., 2010), previous attempts at proving hardness of approximation, including those under average case assumptions, fail to achieve a polynomial ratio; the best ratios ruled out under any worst case assumption and any average case assumption are only any constant (Raghavendra and Steurer, 2010) and $2^{\Omega(\log^{2/3} n)}$ (Alon et al., 2011) respectively. In this work, we propose the Almost-Exponential Time Hypothesis (Almost-ETH), which postulates that no algorithm can solve 3SAT on $n$ variables in $O(2^{n^{1 - \gamma}})$ time for any constant $\gamma > 0$. Assuming Almost-ETH, we show that, for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$, there is no polynomial-time algorithm that approximates {\sc D$k$S} to within $2^{(\log n)^{1 - \varepsilon}}$ factor of the optimum. In addition, our result has perfect completeness, meaning that, assuming Almost-ETH, no polynomial-time algorithm can even distinguish between the case in which $G$ contains a $k$-clique and the case in which every induced $k$-subgraph of $G$ has density at most $2^{-(\log n)^{1 - \varepsilon}}$.

papers.title: Optimal Inapproximability of Satisfiable $k$-LIN over Non-Abelian Groups
papers.abstract: A seminal result of H\r{a}stad [J. ACM, 48(4):798--859, 2001] shows that it is NP-hard to find an assignment that satisfies $\frac{1}{|G|}+\varepsilon$ fraction of the constraints of a given $k$-LIN instance over an abelian group, even if there is an assignment that satisfies $(1-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the constraints, for any constant $\varepsilon>0$. Engebretsen et al. [Theoretical Computer Science, 312(1):17--45, 2004] later showed that the same hardness result holds for $k$-LIN instances over any finite non-abelian group. Unlike the abelian case, where we can efficiently find a solution if the instance is satisfiable, in the non-abelian case, it is NP-complete to decide if a given system of linear equations is satisfiable or not, as shown by Goldmann and Russell [Information and Computation, 178(1):253--262. 2002]. Surprisingly, for certain non-abelian groups $G$, given a satisfiable $k$-LIN instance over $G$, one can in fact do better than just outputting a random assignment using a simple but clever algorithm. The approximation factor achieved by this algorithm varies with the underlying group. In this paper, we show that this algorithm is {\em optimal} by proving a tight hardness of approximation of satisfiable $k$-LIN instance over {\em any} non-abelian $G$, assuming $P \neq NP$. As a corollary, we also get $3$-query probabilistically checkable proofs with perfect completeness over large alphabets with improved soundness. Our proof crucially uses structural properties captured by Gowers' notion of {\em quasi-randomness} for non-abelian groups [Combinatorics, Probability and Computing, 17(3):363--387, 2008].

papers.title: Polynomial and Hyperplane Avoidance over the Integers with Applications to Integer-Point Counting
papers.abstract: We study the \emph{Polynomial Avoidance Problem}: given a finite collection $F \subseteq Z[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ of nonzero polynomials, find a vector $x \in Z^n$ of minimum $\ell_p$-norm such that $f(x)\neq0$ for every $f \in F$. Each polynomial is given sparsely as a list of its nonzero terms. The affine special case is the \emph{Hyperplane Avoidance Problem}. This special case arises in Barvinok-type algorithms for counting integer points in polyhedra, when certain rational generating functions must be evaluated at a removable singularity. Our main results are as follows: 1) Let $D:=\sum_{f\in F} \text{deg} f$. Every instance admits a feasible vector $x$ satisfying \[ \|x\|_1 \leq \min\left\{D,\frac{D+n}{2}\right\}. \] This bound is tight. Such a vector can be found by a deterministic algorithm whose bit complexity is polynomial in $D$ and the sparse encoding length of the input. Our proof uses a new algorithmic variant of the \emph{Combinatorial Nullstellensatz}; 2) In the affine case, with $m$ input polynomials, such a vector can be constructed by a fast deterministic polynomial-time algorithm using $O(nm)$ arithmetic operations. For the homogeneous case, Barvinok's original approach provides only the weaker guarantee $\|x\|_1 = O((nm)^{n-1})$; 3) The problem is NP-hard for every $p\in R_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\}$, even for homogeneous linear forms; 4) As an application, we improve the complexity bound for counting integer points in general rational polytopes. We also improve the bound for polyhedra of bounded codimension; this includes the counting version of the \emph{Unbounded Subset-Sum} problem as a special case.

papers.title: The Counting General Dominating Set Framework
papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework of counting problems called #GDS that generalizes #$(\sigma, \rho)$-Set, a class of domination-type problems that includes counting dominating sets and counting total dominating sets. We explore the intricate relation between #GDS and the well-known Holant framework. We adapt the technique of gadget construction of Holant to the #GDS framework; using this technique, we prove the #P-completeness of counting dominating sets for 3-regular planar bipartite simple graphs. Using interpolation for powered Holant problems and a special reduction method via symmetric bipartite graphs, we also prove the #P-completeness of counting total dominating sets for the same graph class.

papers.title: Even more properties of parity based bit-counting complexity classes
papers.abstract: We investigate several additional properties of parity based bit-counting complexity classes ${\bf B_{|0|\oplus}P}$ and ${\bf B_{|1|\oplus}P}$. We first prove that ${\bf C_=P}={\bf ES}={\bf MNS}\subseteq{\bf P}^{{\bf B_{|1|\oplus}P}}={\bf P}^{{\bf B_{|0|\oplus}P}}$. We then build upon the four consecutive value theorem from \cite{P26b} and develop a bit recovery procedure that reconstructs the binary representation of a ${\bf \#P}$ value one bit at a time by querying appropriately padded and shifted versions of that value. Using this procedure, we prove that ${\bf PP}\subseteq{\bf P}^{{\bf B_{|1|\oplus}P}}$ and ${\bf PP}\subseteq{\bf P}^{{\bf B_{|0|\oplus}P}}$, which consequently yields ${\bf P}^{\bf PP}={\bf P}^{\bf B_{|0|\oplus}P}={\bf P}^{\bf B_{|1|\oplus}P}$. Furthermore, since this procedure recovers the complete numerical output of a ${\bf \#P}$ function, it also establishes the functional containments of ${\bf \#P}\subseteq{\bf FP}^{{\bf B_{|1|\oplus}P}}$ and ${\bf \#P}\subseteq{\bf FP}^{{\bf B_{|0|\oplus}P}}$. We additionally demonstrate that caching repeated oracle queries reduces the number of distinct queries required for the bit recovery procedure from $4n$ to $2n+2$. Finally, we prove that parity based bit-counting hierarchies ${\bf \Sigma B_{|0|\oplus}H}$, ${\bf \Sigma B_{|1|\oplus}H}$, ${\bf \Delta B_{|0|\oplus}H}$ and ${\bf \Delta B_{|1|\oplus}H}$ contain ${\bf CH}$. As a result, these hierarchies coincide with ${\bf CH}$ since the reverse containments were already established in \cite{P26b}.

papers.title: Entrywise Logarithmic Matrix Algebra and Dichotomy of Planar Graph Homomorphisms
papers.abstract: We prove a complexity classification of counting planar graph homomorphisms with non-negative weights. For a real symmetric matrix $M$ with nonnegative entries, the problem $\GH(M)$ is either (1) P-time computable over all graphs, or (2) \#P-hard in general but P-time computable over planar graphs, or (3) \#P-hard over planar graphs. Furthermore, $\GH(M)$ in (2) consists of precisely those that involve the P-time FKT algorithm to count planar perfect matchings with a holographic transformation. The dichotomy for entrywise positive and full rank matrices lies at the core of the proof. In this setting, the main tool is a matrix algebra ${A}$ (a vector space with bilinear multiplication) formed by taking the real span of (centered) entrywise logarithms of all realizable matrices from $M$ using planar edge gadgets and polynomial interpolation. We then define a multiplicative homomorphism $F(\cdot)$ on the algebra ${A}$, which turns out to be a polynomial map. The exponents of prime factorization of component polynomials of $F$ induce graph distances for distance-regular graphs. These graphs are either the Hamming graphs or Doob graphs using a classification result for distance-regular graphs (if $\PlGH(M)$ is not \#P-hard), after obtaining their intersection numbers. The dichotomy is proved in either case. We then extend the complexity classification to all nonnegative matrices.

papers.title: PSPACE-Completeness of the Reachability Relation of Robust Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: Dynamical systems are a widely used model of computation and an intuitive representation of many natural phenomena in many applied fields. The last decades have seen an impressive use of computers in studying and analysing them, with several visible theoretical breakthroughs. The question of reachability for dynamical systems is central: given two points, is there a trajectory between them in the dynamical system? Reachability, in particular over the reals, is undecidable in the general case: it is only computably enumerable, even under reasonable hypotheses, e.g. for a computable dynamics in general. But it is known to become decidable, and even lies in PSPACE, under suitably quantified robustness assumptions. In this paper, we focus on PSPACE-completeness results over the reals, in the sense of computable analysis, regarding discrete-time and continuous-time robust dynamical systems. We prove that, under some additional and rather reasonable hypotheses, the reachability relation becomes even PSPACE-complete for both classical and second-order complexity second-order complexity, for an adapted notion of reduction. As a side-effect, we also prove an improvement of an algebraic Ordinary Differential Equations-based characterisation of PSPACE, removing one of the base functions of the algebra. By doing so, we link results from dynamical systems and complexity over the reals, including the models of computable analysis and second-order complexity.
